results.title: Enhancing Missile Defence: Robustness to Sensor Dropouts
results.content: Enhancing Missile Defence: Robustness to Sensor Dropouts. # Enhancing Missile Defence: Robustness to Sensor Dropouts. Enhancing Missile Defence: Robustness to Sensor Dropouts. As we transition to discussing sensor dropouts, it becomes clear that the reliability of these systems must be continuously ensured, as any failure in detection technology can compromise the entire missile defence strategy, highlighting the need for enhanced robustness in these systems. The ability of missile defence systems to operate effectively amidst sensor malfunctions is an essential consideration for national defense strategies. Overall, the integration of predictive modeling in missile defence not only enhances operational readiness but also fortifies the resilience of defense systems against sensor failures. By predicting the future state of a missile’s trajectory based on its last known position and velocity, the Kalman filter allows missile defence systems to continue tracking, albeit with reduced accuracy, during sensor outages. Through the combination of Kalman filtering, machine learning techniques, and sophisticated data fusion strategies, missile defence systems can effectively sustain track during sensor dropout events, thereby enhancing their operational reliability and effectiveness in neutralizing potential threats. In enhancing missile defence, the integration of redundant sensors plays a pivotal role in ensuring that the system remains robust in the face of potential sensor dropouts. Design considerations are paramount when integrating redundant sensors into missile defence systems. Ultimately, the integration of redundant sensors is a strategic measure that significantly enhances missile defence systems’ resilience. Modern missile defence systems require high levels of accuracy, particularly in real-time tracking scenarios where sensor data may be incomplete due to dropouts or interruptions. As a result, missile defence systems become more resilient, allowing operators to maintain situational awareness and effective decision-making capabilities even during interruptions in sensor data. Overall, the use of adaptive algorithms in missile tracking not only strengthens the operational capabilities of defence systems but also reinforces the strategic advantage during critical engagements. The realm of missile defence technology is continuously evolving, particularly regarding the resilience of systems to sensor dropouts. Ongoing research and development initiatives are focusing on these innovations to create missile defence systems that are robust and capable of adapting to unforeseen challenges, such as sensor dropouts.

results.title: Impact of Phonetics on Speaker Identity in Adversarial ...
results.content: Impact of Phonetics on Speaker Identity in Adversarial Voice Attack Daniyal Kabir Dar, Qiben Yan, Li Xiao, Arun Ross Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Michigan State University, USA {dardaniy, qyan, lxiao, rossarun}@msu.edu Abstract—Adversarial perturbations in speech pose a serious threat to automatic speech recognition (ASR) and speaker verification by introducing subtle waveform modifications that remain imperceptible to humans but can significantly alter system outputs. While targeted attacks on end-to-end ASR models have been widely studied, the phonetic basis of these perturbations and their effect on speaker identity remain underexplored. Results across 16 phonet-ically diverse target phrases demonstrate that adversarial audio induces both transcription errors and identity drift, highlighting the need for phonetic-aware defenses to ensure the robustness of ASR and speaker recognition systems. The Automatic Speaker Recognition (ASR) model yields adversarial transcriptions, while the Speaker Identification (SID) model produces embeddings that drift from the source identity, degrading similarity. The contributions of this work are threefold: (i) we pro-vide a phonetic-level analysis of adversarial audio, revealing how perturbations exploit systematic phoneme confusions; (ii) we utilize the concept of identity drift, characterizing how adversarial perturbations alter phonetic cues underlying speaker identity; and (iii) we conduct extensive experiments on DeepSpeech and evaluate speaker verification metrics (gen-uine vs. RELATED WORK We evaluate the effect of adversarial perturbations on speaker identity using two state-of-the-art embedding models: arXiv:2509.15437v1 [cs.SD] 18 Sep 2025 ECAPA-TDNN [3] and a ResNet-based speaker verification backbone [4], [5]. Speaker verification systems face similar threats: early works demonstrated targeted attacks against i-vector and DNN-based SV [16], [17], [18], with extensions to universal perturbations [9], robust real-time variants [17], and stress-testing embedding models [19], [20], [21]. CONCLUSION We present a phonetic perspective on adversarial attacks in the audio domain, demonstrating that perturbations not only mislead automatic speech recognition but also distort speaker embeddings in ways that compromise biometric verification. By systematically evaluating 16 phonetically diverse target phrases, we utilize the concept of identity drift, showing that adversarial audio shifts speaker embeddings toward impostor space, significantly degrading the separability of genuine and impostor samples and that identity drift is strongly correlated with phonetic complexity and utterance length: short vowel-rich commands remained robust, while fricative-heavy, cluster-rich pangrams exhibited severe degradation in verification performance.

results.title: Adversarial attacks and robustness for tabular data
results.content: ## Sign in to view more content. # Adversarial attacks and robustness for tabular data. Over the last years, deep learning has become the predominant approach to learning predictive models from data. In this blog post, we discuss so-called adversarial attacks in the context of tabular data. While most of the research in this area focuses on image classification problems, such attacks are of utmost relevance for tabular data as well. Ten years ago, researchers identified adversarial attacks as an unexpected failure mode of neural networks [Szegedy et al., 2014]. Imperceptible perturbations of the input data can be often constructed in such a way that they fool the model into making incorrect predictions. The image on the right has been adversarially attacked such that the introduced perturbations are too small to be visually detected (maximally 1% of the standard deviation for each pixel). A robust classification model should therefore make the same prediction on the original and the modified image. While robustness and security considerations are important for all types of ML models and data modalities, the abovementioned issues complicate the analysis especially for tabular data. They take sparsity and other feature constraints into account in order to establish meaningful adversarial attacks in the context of tabular data. We will demonstrate how adversarial robustness establishes a relevant criterion for assessing a model's performance in addition to the classical metrics. At this point, adversarial robustness opens a complementary perspective on the model performances. This way the ASR establishes a measure of a model's adversarial vulnerability or the lack of robustness. But then again, model 3 is both more accurate and more robust than model 2. The role of the robustness tests in such situations is to establish the quantitative basis for such model selection decisions. For a real-world deployment, in addition to other relevant criteria such as fairness, it is therefore important to test the robustness of ML models with respect to adversarial attacks. results.content: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), which are pretrained on large-scale, cross-domain data and capable of zero-shot forecasting in new scenarios without further training, are increasingly adopted in real-world applications. However, as the zero-shot forecasting paradigm gets popular, a critical yet overlooked question emerges: Are TSFMs robust to adversarial input perturbations? To address this gap, we conduct a systematic investigation into the adversarial robustness of TSFMs. Our results show that even minimal perturbations can induce significant and controllable changes in forecast behaviors, including trend reversal, temporal drift, and amplitude shift, posing serious risks to TSFM-based services.
